analysis.one_liner: Cracks down on gun traffickers and rogue dealers and builds a national ballistics database of new guns.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 84 sponsors, 81 of them Democrats, in March 2000 but never left the House Judiciary Committee and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The ENFORCE Act targeted the supply side of illegal guns rather than gun owners generally. It presumed that anyone selling large numbers of guns was a dealer subject to licensing, required dealers to operate from a real storefront instead of a home, allowed federal inspections of dealer records four times a year instead of once, required thefts of guns from shipping companies to be reported, and created a national database by requiring every new gun to be test-fired and its ballistics signature recorded. It also authorized roughly $385 million for background-check record improvements, 600 new ATF agents, 114 federal prosecutors, grants for local gun prosecutors, and research on 'smart gun' technology.
analysis.who_benefits: People living in communities with high rates of gun violence, since the bill aimed at traffickers who funnel guns to criminals and at rogue dealers; police and prosecutors also gain tools and funding.

how_it_helps.text: It presumed that anyone selling more than 50 guns in a year, or more than 30 in 30 days, was acting as a dealer and needed a license, closing a common trafficking loophole while exempting family gifts and inheritances [S2][S3].
It required dealers to operate from a fixed storefront open to the public rather than a private residence, targeting unlicensed 'kitchen-table' sellers [S2][S3].
It required licensed manufacturers and importers to test-fire every new gun and file its ballistics fingerprint in a computerized database police could search to trace crime guns [S2][S3].

It authorized funding for 600 ATF agents and inspectors, 114 federal firearms prosecutors, grants to state and local gun prosecutors, and improvements to criminal records — especially domestic violence records — fed into the national background check system [S3].

It let the Treasury suspend licenses, revoke them, or impose civil fines up to $10,000 for dealer violations, and quadrupled permissible warrantless record inspections from once to four times a year [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Licensed gun dealers and manufacturers would bear compliance costs — storefronts, secure storage, recordkeeping, and test-firing every gun — and taxpayers would fund roughly $385 million in authorized spending. Shipping companies would face fines up to $10,000 for failing to report stolen firearms.

drawbacks.text: The fixed-premises requirement would have ended the ability of small or hobbyist dealers to operate from their homes, imposing real costs on low-volume dealers [S3].

It would have permanently barred people convicted of violent felonies or serious drug offenses from possessing firearms even if their conviction was expunged or their civil rights restored, unless the restoring authority expressly found them safe — a provision gun-rights and civil-liberties critics could object to as overly rigid [S2][S3].

The ballistics test-firing mandate applied to every gun a manufacturer or importer transferred, a compliance burden the bill offset only partially with federal equipment funding, and it limited judicial review of regulatory penalties [S2][S3].
The bill authorized about $385 million in new federal spending for fiscal 2001, a cost an honest supporter would have to defend [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core enforcement provisions — closing the high-volume-seller loophole, storefront licensing, and ballistics tracing — aim squarely at the small share of dealers who supply most crime guns, and the funded investigators and prosecutors give them teeth. The serious costs fall on compliant dealers and manufacturers in paperwork and premises expenses, and the lifetime ban for expunged felony convictions raises a genuine fairness question. On balance the benefits to public safety outweigh the compliance burdens, though the enforcement-first design means its impact depends entirely on funding actually being appropriated.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee, then to its Crime subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Carolyn McCarthy of New York introduced the ENFORCE Act on March 22, 2000, with 83 cosponsors — 81 Democrats and 2 Republicans [S1][S4].
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction [S1][S5].
On April 4, 2000, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime, where the record ends; no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, so the bill died in subcommittee without a vote in either chamber [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun dealers and manufacturers were better off, avoiding new licensing, storage, inspection, and ballistics-testing requirements. No new anti-trafficking enforcement was added either.

against.what_they_did: Opposed expanded dealer regulation and ballistics 'fingerprinting' measures of this kind during this period, and congressional Republicans aligned with that position on gun bills in the 106th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 81 of 83 cosponsors were Democrats, with only 2 Republicans — and the bill never advanced in a Republican-controlled House.

industries.note: The bill would have required storefront premises, secure inventory storage, quadrupled inspections, and a presumption of dealer status at 50 guns sold a year, all aimed at closing the unlicensed-seller loophole that supplies illegal guns. Dealers' interest in avoiding these rules ran against the enforcement goal the bill served for the public.

Every gun would have had to be test-fired and its ballistics signature filed in a national police database before sale, with fines up to $10,000 per violation. The industry's resistance to a permanent tracing record of its products ran against the investigative tool the public would gain.

Carriers would have faced civil fines up to $10,000 for failing to report a stolen or lost firearm within 48 hours. The cost to carriers buys faster recovery of stolen guns, so their interest in avoiding the mandate runs against the public's.

industries.industry: Federal and state law enforcement agencies
industries.note: The bill authorized 600 new ATF agents, 114 federal prosecutors, and grants for state and local gun prosecutors and record improvements. More enforcement capacity against traffickers serves the same public the bill targets.
